tool.name: Optuna
tool.tagline: Define-by-run hyperparameter optimization with smart sampling and pruning
tool.description: Optuna is a Python framework for hyperparameter optimization. You write an objective function that asks a trial for parameter values and returns a score; Optuna's samplers (TPE, CMA-ES, Gaussian processes and more) choose promising values, and pruners stop unpromising trials early. It scales from a notebook to many parallel workers sharing a database, with built-in visualization and multi-objective support.

glossary.def: In Optuna, the function you write that receives a trial, uses the values it suggests (usually to train and score a model) and returns the score to optimize.
The formula that scores how wrong a model's predictions are; training tries to make it as small as possible.
In Optuna, one of the settings being tuned, such as a learning rate; every trial gets a value for each. (In plain Python, a parameter is a named input of a function.)
In Optuna, one call of the objective function with one set of suggested values, together with its result.
In Optuna, one whole search for the best settings: all its trials, the direction (minimize or maximize) and the sampler and pruner it uses.
All the values a tuning run is allowed to try: each setting with its range or list of choices.
Optuna's style of describing the search space: there is no separate list; the space is whatever the objective function asks for while it runs.
The part of Optuna that picks the values each new trial gets, for example at random or by learning from earlier trials.
Optuna's default sampler. It splits finished trials into good and bad ones and picks new values that look like the good ones and unlike the bad ones.
A scale where each step multiplies instead of adds (0.001, 0.01, 0.1), so every order of magnitude gets equal room.
A search space where some settings exist only when another setting has a certain value, like a tree depth only when the model is a tree.
Optuna's read-only record of a trial: its number, suggested values, score, state and timing.
An extra named value you attach to an Optuna trial or study with set_user_attr, such as a second score or a file path.
Stopping a trial early because its in-between scores already look worse than other trials', so the time goes to more promising ones.
The part of Optuna that decides whether a running trial should be stopped early, for example MedianPruner or HyperbandPruner.
A score a trial reports partway through, such as after each round of training, so a pruner can judge it early.
The table type of the pandas library: named columns and numbered rows, like a spreadsheet inside a Python program.
The most popular Python library for classic machine learning. Every model in it is trained with fit() and used with predict().
Scoring a model by splitting the data into parts, training several times with a different part held back for scoring, and averaging the scores.
Where an Optuna study is saved so it survives restarts and can be shared: a database or a journal file. RDBStorage and JournalStorage are the two kinds.
A small 'still alive' signal a running trial writes to storage at a regular interval, so trials whose worker died can be detected.
A trial still marked as running whose heartbeat stopped long ago, meaning its worker almost certainly died.
A statistical model that predicts the score of untried values from tried ones, together with how unsure it is about each prediction.
An evolution strategy for tuning decimal settings: it keeps a cloud of candidate points and repeatedly moves and reshapes it toward better scores.
A search method that imitates evolution: keep the best candidates, mix and slightly change them to make new ones, and repeat.
Trying every combination of a fixed list of values for each setting.
Trying settings chosen at random within their ranges; a simple, surprisingly strong baseline.
Search methods that use the results of earlier trials to build a model of where good values probably are, and try those next.
With several goals at once, the set of options that no other option beats on every goal at the same time: the best possible trade-offs.
Optimizing several scores at once, such as accuracy and speed, instead of a single one.
In statistics, a small bump-shaped curve placed on each observed value; adding the bumps together gives a smooth picture of where values are common.
A curve showing how likely each value is: high where values are common, low where they are rare.
How much a candidate is expected to beat the best score found so far, averaged over what its score might turn out to be.
A pruning strategy that gives many trials a small budget, keeps only the best fraction, gives those more, and so on.
A saved copy of a model partway through training, so you can keep the best version or resume later.

concepts.name: Objective, trial and study
concepts.summary: Write an objective function, create a study, run optimize, and read the best settings found.
concepts.why: These three objects are the whole Optuna mental model; everything else builds on them.
concepts.body:
Many programs have settings you must pick by hand, where the best values aren't obvious. The classic case is **machine learning**: programs that learn patterns from example data instead of following hand-written rules.

The learning step is called **training**, and the settings you choose before it starts, such as how complex the model may get, are **hyperparameters**. The usual way to find good ones is to try many combinations and keep the one that scores best. Optuna automates that search.

Optuna is built on three ideas. The first is the **objective function**, a function you write. It receives a **trial** object, asks it for values for the settings, uses them (usually it trains a model and measures how good it is) and returns a number: the score.

A trial is one call of the objective with one set of values. A call like `trial.suggest_float("x", -10, 10)` does two things: it tells Optuna the allowed range, and it returns the value Optuna picked for this trial.

A **study** is the whole search. `optuna.create_study(direction="minimize")` creates one; use `"maximize"` when higher scores are better, like accuracy (the share of correct answers). `study.optimize(objective, n_trials=100)` then runs 100 trials.

Afterwards:

- `study.best_params` is a dict of the best values found,
- `study.best_value` is the best score,
- `study.best_trial` is the full record of that trial (a `FrozenTrial`): its number, values, notes and timing.

Optuna prints one line of information per trial. Silence it with `optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)`.

How does Optuna pick values? Its default **sampler**, the part that chooses each trial's values, is **TPE**. It looks at finished trials, learns which ranges tend to score well, and tries more values there. That usually finds better settings in the same number of trials than going through a fixed grid of combinations or picking purely at random.

Make the objective give the same score for the same values where you can: use fixed data and a fixed **random seed** (the starting number for random choices; the same seed gives the same choices). Otherwise luck can make an ordinary trial look best.
concepts.code:
import optuna

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)   # no per-trial messages

def objective(trial):
    x = trial.suggest_float("x", -10, 10)     # a decimal between -10 and 10
    y = trial.suggest_int("y", -5, 5)         # a whole number between -5 and 5
    return (x - 2) ** 2 + (y + 1) ** 2         # a made-up score, smallest at x=2, y=-1

study = optuna.create_study(direction="minimize",
                            sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=0))
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=60)

print(study.best_params)          # close to {'x': 2.0, 'y': -1}
print(round(study.best_value, 2)) # close to 0
print(len(study.trials))          # 60
takeaways: The objective function takes a trial, asks it for values and returns a score
`create_study(direction=...)` then `optimize(objective, n_trials=...)`
Read `best_params`, `best_value` and `best_trial` afterwards
pitfalls: Forgetting direction='maximize' when returning accuracy, so Optuna searches for the worst settings.

quiz.q: Your objective returns the model's accuracy (share of correct answers). What must you set?
quiz.explain: Studies minimize by default; accuracy must be maximized.

concepts.name: Search spaces with suggest
concepts.summary: Ask for decimal, log-scale, whole-number, stepped and multiple-choice settings, including settings that depend on others.
concepts.why: The search space decides what Optuna can find; log scales and conditional settings make the search efficient.
concepts.body:
The **search space** is the set of all values Optuna may try. Optuna is **define-by-run**: the search space is simply whatever your objective asks for while it runs, so ordinary Python code controls it.

The suggest functions:

- `trial.suggest_float(name, low, high)` for decimal numbers. Add `step=0.1` to allow only multiples of 0.1.
- `trial.suggest_int(name, low, high)` for whole numbers, also with `step=` or `log=True` (e.g. a number of trees from 16 to 1024).
- `trial.suggest_categorical(name, choices)` to pick from a list of options; choices can be `None`, bools, ints, floats or strings.

Some settings span several orders of magnitude. A **learning rate**, for example, controls how big each learning step of a model is, and good values range from 0.00001 to 0.1. Pass `log=True` to search such a range on a **log scale**: 0.00001 to 0.0001, 0.0001 to 0.001 and so on each get an equal share of trials.

Ranges include both ends. Each setting name must keep the same range in every trial; asking for `"lr"` with different ranges in different trials causes an error or a warning.

A **conditional search space**, where some settings exist only for certain choices, is just an `if`:

```python
kind = trial.suggest_categorical("kind", ["tree", "linear"])
if kind == "tree":
    depth = trial.suggest_int("tree_depth", 2, 32, log=True)
else:
    c = trial.suggest_float("linear_c", 1e-3, 1e3, log=True)
```

Each trial records only the settings it actually asked for. Loops work too: ask for a count `n`, then ask for one setting per item, named `units_0`, `units_1` and so on.

Keep ranges realistic: a range that is too wide wastes trials, while one that is too narrow may leave out the best value. If the best value lands at the edge of its range, widen the range.
concepts.code:
import optuna

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)

def objective(trial):
    model = trial.suggest_categorical("model", ["linear", "mlp"])
    lr = trial.suggest_float("lr", 1e-5, 1e-1, log=True)       # learning rate, log scale
    if model == "mlp":                                         # only this model has layers
        n_layers = trial.suggest_int("n_layers", 1, 3)
        widths = [trial.suggest_int(f"units_{i}", 16, 256, log=True)
                  for i in range(n_layers)]                     # one setting per layer
        cost = abs(lr - 1e-3) * 100 + abs(sum(widths) - 200) / 100
    else:
        cost = abs(lr - 1e-2) * 100 + 1.0
    return cost                                                 # made-up score to minimize

study = optuna.create_study(sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=1))
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=40)
t = study.trials[0]
print(sorted(t.params))       # only the settings this trial asked for
print(study.best_params["model"])   # mlp
takeaways: Suggest calls define the search space as the objective runs
Use `log=True` for settings that span orders of magnitude, like learning rates
Ordinary `if` statements and loops create conditional search spaces
pitfalls: Giving the same setting name different ranges in different branches, which conflicts with what Optuna recorded for it.

quiz.q: Which call is most appropriate for a learning rate between 1e-5 and 1e-1?
quiz.explain: A log scale gives each order of magnitude an equal share of trials; a plain range would almost never try the small values.

concepts.name: Inspecting trials and results
concepts.summary: Look at every trial's values, score, state and timing, attach extra notes, and export everything to a pandas table.
concepts.why: The best score is only part of the story; the trial history shows failures, sensitivity and where to search next.
concepts.body:
`study.trials` is a list of **FrozenTrial** objects: read-only records of the trials. Each has `number`, `params` (the values it got), `value` (its score; `values` when there are several scores), `state`, start and end times, `duration`, `user_attrs`, and any in-between scores it reported for **pruning** (stopping bad trials early; a later lesson).

**States** tell you what happened:

- `COMPLETE`: returned a score.
- `PRUNED`: stopped early by pruning.
- `FAIL`: the objective raised an exception, or returned None or NaN.
- `RUNNING`, and `WAITING` (queued with `enqueue_trial`).

**NaN** ("not a number") is the special float value for a result that isn't a valid number, such as 0 divided by 0 in decimal maths.

Filter with `study.get_trials(states=(optuna.trial.TrialState.COMPLETE,))`.

`study.trials_dataframe()` returns a **DataFrame**, the table type of the popular pandas library, with columns like `number`, `value`, `params_lr`, `state` and `duration`. It's the quickest way to sort, group or plot results.

Store extra information on a trial with `trial.set_user_attr("val_f1", f1)`: a second score, the point in training where the score peaked, or where a saved model is. These **user attributes** appear as `user_attrs_*` columns. Notes for the whole study go in `study.set_user_attr`.

If the objective raises an exception, the trial is marked `FAIL` and, by default, the exception reaches your code and stops `optimize`. Pass `catch=(ValueError,)` to record such failures and carry on. Returning `float("nan")` also marks the trial as failed without stopping the study.
concepts.code:
import optuna

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)

def objective(trial):
    x = trial.suggest_float("x", 0, 4)
    if x > 3.5:
        raise ValueError("unstable region")      # becomes a FAIL trial
    trial.set_user_attr("x_squared", x * x)
    return (x - 1) ** 2

study = optuna.create_study(sampler=optuna.samplers.RandomSampler(seed=0))
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=20, catch=(ValueError,))

df = study.trials_dataframe()
print(df["state"].value_counts().to_dict())   # e.g. {'COMPLETE': 18, 'FAIL': 2}
print(df.sort_values("value").iloc[0][["params_x", "user_attrs_x_squared"]].round(2).to_dict())

done = study.get_trials(states=(optuna.trial.TrialState.COMPLETE,))
print(all(t.value is not None for t in done))  # True
takeaways: `study.trials` holds FrozenTrials with params, value, state and timing
`trials_dataframe()` exports everything to a pandas DataFrame
Use `set_user_attr` for extra scores; `catch=` keeps the study going after errors
pitfalls: Letting one bad configuration's exception abort a long study instead of using catch= or returning NaN.

quiz.q: An objective raises ZeroDivisionError for some parameters and you call optimize(..., catch=(ZeroDivisionError,)). What happens on that error?
options: The trial is recorded as PRUNED
The trial is recorded as FAIL and optimization continues
The trial is retried with the same parameters
quiz.explain: Caught exceptions mark the trial FAIL and the study proceeds with the next trial.

concepts.name: Tuning a real model
concepts.summary: Tune a scikit-learn model with cross-validation inside the objective, then retrain it with the best settings.
concepts.why: This is the everyday use of Optuna and the pattern for tuning any model.
concepts.body:
Time for a real model. **scikit-learn** is Python's most popular library for classic machine learning. Every model in it works the same way: create it with its hyperparameters, train it with `fit(X, y)` on inputs `X` and correct answers `y`, then use it with `predict` or measure it with `score`.

A realistic objective:

1. Asks the trial for hyperparameters.
2. Builds the model with them.
3. Scores it on data it wasn't trained on, ideally with cross-validation.
4. Returns the average score.

**Cross-validation** splits the data into, say, 5 parts. It trains 5 times, each time holding back a different part to score on, and averages the 5 scores. That's slower than a single split but depends far less on luck. `cross_val_score` does it in one call:

```python
def objective(trial):
    params = {"n_estimators": trial.suggest_int("n_estimators", 50, 400),
              "max_depth": trial.suggest_int("max_depth", 2, 16)}
    return cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(**params), X, y, cv=5).mean()
```

Keep a **test set** apart from the start: examples the study never sees. After optimization, retrain on the rest of the data (the **training data**) with `study.best_params`, then score once on the test set. Using the test set inside the objective leaks information, so the final score looks better than the model really is.

Practical tips:

- Load data outside the objective (or pass it in with a closure or `functools.partial`) so it isn't reloaded every trial.
- Fix the model's random seed so results can be repeated.
- `n_jobs` lets a model or `cross_val_score` use several of the computer's cores at once. Set it in one place, not both, or they compete for the same cores.
- Start with a modest budget (50 to 100 trials) and look at the results before scaling up.

Optuna doesn't care what the model is: the same pattern works for XGBoost, PyTorch or any code that produces a score.
concepts.code:
import optuna
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, train_test_split

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)
X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
# keep 20% aside as the test set; the study only sees X_tr, y_tr
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)

def objective(trial):
    params = {
        "n_estimators": trial.suggest_int("n_estimators", 50, 300, step=50),
        "max_depth": trial.suggest_int("max_depth", 2, 16, log=True),
        "max_features": trial.suggest_categorical("max_features", ["sqrt", "log2", None]),
    }
    model = RandomForestClassifier(**params, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1)
    return cross_val_score(model, X_tr, y_tr, cv=3).mean()   # average of 3 scores

study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize")
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=15)

final = RandomForestClassifier(**study.best_params, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"cv={study.best_value:.3f} test={final.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")  # both about 0.95
takeaways: Score with cross-validation inside the objective
Retrain with `best_params` and test once on data the study never saw
Load data once, outside the objective
pitfalls: Scoring on the test set inside the objective, which tunes the settings to the test set and inflates the final score.

quiz.q: Why score on a separate test set after the study instead of reporting study.best_value?
options: best_value is too optimistic: it is the luckiest of many slightly noisy scores
quiz.explain: Picking the best of many noisy scores overstates how good the model is; an untouched test set gives an honest estimate.

concepts.name: Choosing a sampler
concepts.summary: Pick between TPE, random, CMA-ES, Gaussian-process, grid and QMC samplers, and seed them so results can be repeated.
concepts.why: The sampler is the search method; the right one can halve the number of trials you need.
concepts.body:
The sampler decides which values each trial gets. Pass one to `create_study(sampler=...)`. Most of Optuna's samplers do **Bayesian optimization**: they use earlier results to model where good values probably are, and try there next.

- `TPESampler` (default): robust, handles conditional and multiple-choice settings, and scales to thousands of trials. In Optuna 5 it models all settings together (multivariate) by default for single-objective studies. An Expert lesson shows how it works.
- `GPSampler`: uses a **Gaussian process**. Very efficient for small budgets (tens of trials) when most settings are decimal numbers; slower per trial, and needs PyTorch and SciPy installed.
- `CmaEsSampler`: **CMA-ES**, an evolution strategy (needs the `cmaes` package). Strong for decimal settings with larger budgets; multiple-choice settings are sampled at random instead.

- `RandomSampler`: **random search**, a useful baseline and good for broad first exploration.
- `QMCSampler`: quasi-random points, which cover the space more evenly than truly random ones.
- `GridSampler(search_space)`: a **grid search** through every combination, when you really need all of them.
- `NSGAIISampler`/`NSGAIIISampler`: **genetic algorithms**, for studies with several scores to optimize at once (an Advanced lesson).

Model-based samplers start with `n_startup_trials` random trials (10 for TPE) before they build their model, so tiny budgets behave like random search.

Pass `seed=` to get the same sequence again when trials run one after another. When several trials run at the same time, results can't be repeated exactly, because trials finish in a varying order.

Rules of thumb: under about 100 trials with mostly decimal settings, try `GPSampler`; otherwise TPE. Compare samplers on your own problem with a few seeds before committing.
concepts.code:
import optuna

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)

def objective(trial):
    x = trial.suggest_float("x", -5, 5)
    y = trial.suggest_float("y", -5, 5)
    return (x - 1) ** 2 + (y + 2) ** 2

samplers = {
    "random": optuna.samplers.RandomSampler(seed=0),
    "tpe": optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=0),
    "cmaes": optuna.samplers.CmaEsSampler(seed=0),
    "qmc": optuna.samplers.QMCSampler(seed=0),
}
for name, sampler in samplers.items():
    study = optuna.create_study(sampler=sampler)
    study.optimize(objective, n_trials=60)
    print(f"{name:7} {study.best_value:.4f}")
# model-based tpe and cmaes end much closer to 0 than random or qmc

grid = optuna.samplers.GridSampler({"x": [0, 1, 2], "y": [-2, 0]})
study = optuna.create_study(sampler=grid)
study.optimize(objective)        # stops by itself after all 6 combinations
print(len(study.trials))         # 6
takeaways: TPE is the robust default; a Gaussian process (GPSampler) is efficient for small, mostly-decimal problems
CMA-ES suits decimal settings with bigger budgets; Random and QMC are baselines
Seed samplers to repeat runs where trials run one after another
pitfalls: Comparing samplers with a single seed and tiny budget, where differences are mostly noise.

quiz.q: You can afford only about 30 expensive trials over 5 decimal settings. Which sampler is a strong first choice?
quiz.explain: A Gaussian-process sampler gets the most information out of each trial on small budgets of decimal settings.

concepts.name: Pruning unpromising trials
concepts.summary: Report in-between scores and let a pruner stop bad trials early with MedianPruner, Hyperband and others.
concepts.why: Pruning often cuts tuning time several-fold for models that train in rounds, like neural networks (models made of layers of learned numbers) and boosted trees.
concepts.body:
Many models train in rounds. One full pass over the training data is an **epoch**, and after each one you can measure the model. Many trials are obviously bad after a few epochs; **pruning** stops them early so the time goes to promising ones.

Inside such an objective:

```python
for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    score = train_one_epoch_and_validate()
    trial.report(score, step=epoch)
    if trial.should_prune():
        raise optuna.TrialPruned()
```

`report` records an **intermediate value** (a score partway through); `should_prune` asks the study's **pruner** whether this trial is worse than others at the same step. Raising `optuna.TrialPruned` marks the trial `PRUNED`.

Pruners, set with `create_study(pruner=...)`:

- `MedianPruner` (default): prune if the value is worse than the median (middle value) of earlier trials at the same step. Tune `n_startup_trials` (trials completed before pruning starts) and `n_warmup_steps` (steps before a trial can be pruned).
- `PercentilePruner`: like median, but with a **percentile** you choose (the 25th percentile is the value a quarter of trials fall below).
- `SuccessiveHalvingPruner` and `HyperbandPruner`: give every trial a small budget, keep only the best fraction, give those more, and so on; **Hyperband** is a strong general choice.

- `PatientPruner`: wraps another pruner and waits a few steps without improvement before acting.
- `ThresholdPruner`: prunes when values cross fixed limits, such as a loss that keeps growing.
- `WilcoxonPruner`: for objectives that average a score over many separate cases (like the parts of a cross-validation) rather than over epochs.

Pruning does nothing unless the objective calls `report`. Steps must mean the same thing in every trial (the same epoch numbering).
concepts.code:
import optuna
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)
X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_va, y_tr, y_va = train_test_split(X / 16, y, random_state=0)

def objective(trial):
    alpha = trial.suggest_float("alpha", 1e-6, 1e0, log=True)
    clf = SGDClassifier(alpha=alpha, random_state=0)
    for step in range(20):                       # 20 rounds ("epochs")
        clf.partial_fit(X_tr, y_tr, classes=list(range(10)))
        acc = clf.score(X_va, y_va)
        trial.report(acc, step)
        if trial.should_prune():
            raise optuna.TrialPruned()
    return acc

pruner = optuna.pruners.HyperbandPruner(min_resource=2, max_resource=20)
study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize", pruner=pruner)
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=30)
n_pruned = sum(t.state.name == "PRUNED" for t in study.trials)
print(n_pruned, "of 30 trials pruned")   # typically more than half
print(round(study.best_value, 3))                          # about 0.95
takeaways: Call `trial.report(value, step)` and check `trial.should_prune()` each step
Raise `optuna.TrialPruned()` to stop a trial
MedianPruner is the default; Hyperband is a strong general choice
pitfalls: Setting a pruner but never calling trial.report, so nothing is ever pruned.

quiz.q: You set pruner=MedianPruner() but no trial is ever pruned. What is the most likely cause?
options: The objective never calls trial.report and trial.should_prune
quiz.explain: Pruners act only on reported intermediate values when the objective asks should_prune().

concepts.name: Persistent storage and resuming
concepts.summary: Save studies to SQLite or a journal file, resume them later, and browse them with optuna-dashboard.
concepts.why: Long studies crash, notebooks restart and teams want to see results; saving to storage lets a study survive all that.
concepts.body:
By default a study lives only in your program's memory and disappears when the program ends. Pass a **storage** to save it:

```python
study = optuna.create_study(study_name="rf-tuning", storage="sqlite:///optuna.db",
                            direction="maximize", load_if_exists=True)
```

- `study_name` identifies the study inside the storage.
- `load_if_exists=True` resumes an existing study instead of failing, so the same script can be re-run to add more trials.
- `optuna.load_study(study_name=..., storage=...)` opens a study for analysis elsewhere.

Storage options. The first is a **relational database** (RDB), a **database** that stores records in tables so programs can search and update them quickly: SQLite, PostgreSQL or MySQL, given by an address such as `sqlite:///optuna.db`. SQLite keeps everything in one file and is fine on one machine.

Use PostgreSQL or MySQL, which run as separate database programs, when many **workers** write at the same time. A worker is one running copy of your tuning script; several of them can share one study.

The second is **JournalStorage** with `JournalFileBackend("journal.log")`: a file that new records are only ever added to. It's simple and robust for several workers on one machine or a shared drive, and needs no database program. `JournalRedisBackend` stores the journal in Redis instead.

Utilities: `optuna.get_all_study_names(storage)`, `optuna.delete_study`, `optuna.copy_study`, and the `optuna` terminal command (`optuna studies --storage ...`).

**optuna-dashboard** (`pip install optuna-dashboard`, then `optuna-dashboard sqlite:///optuna.db`) gives a live web page with the history, the importance of each setting, and plots.

Trials interrupted by a crash stay `RUNNING`. Turn on **heartbeats** (`RDBStorage(url, heartbeat_interval=60)`): each running trial then regularly signals that it's alive, and trials that go quiet are marked failed and can optionally be tried again.
concepts.code:
import optuna

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)

def objective(trial):
    x = trial.suggest_float("x", -10, 10)
    return (x - 3) ** 2

storage = "sqlite:///optuna_demo.db"
for session in range(2):                  # e.g. two separate script runs
    study = optuna.create_study(study_name="quadratic", storage=storage,
                                load_if_exists=True)
    study.optimize(objective, n_trials=10)
    print(f"session {session}: {len(study.trials)} trials")
# session 0: 10 trials
# session 1: 20 trials   (resumed)

loaded = optuna.load_study(study_name="quadratic", storage=storage)
print(round(loaded.best_params["x"], 1))  # near 3.0
optuna.delete_study(study_name="quadratic", storage=storage)

from optuna.storages import JournalStorage
from optuna.storages.journal import JournalFileBackend
journal = JournalStorage(JournalFileBackend("optuna_journal.log"))
takeaways: Pass `storage=` and `study_name=` to save a study
`load_if_exists=True` lets the same script resume
SQLite or journal files for one machine; PostgreSQL/MySQL for many workers
pitfalls: Pointing many workers at one SQLite file at the same time, which leads to locking errors.

quiz.q: You rerun a script that calls create_study(study_name='s', storage=url) without load_if_exists. The study already exists. What happens?
options: It silently creates a second study with the same name
It appends trials to the existing study
quiz.explain: Without load_if_exists=True, creating a study whose name already exists in the storage raises an error.

concepts.name: Visualizing studies and importance
concepts.summary: Plot optimization history, parameter importances, slices and contours to understand the search.
concepts.why: Plots reveal which parameters matter, whether the study converged and whether ranges need adjusting.
concepts.body:
`optuna.visualization` builds interactive Plotly figures (and `optuna.visualization.matplotlib` the same plots for Matplotlib). Each takes a study and returns a figure you can `.show()` or save.

- `plot_optimization_history(study)`: objective value per trial with the best-so-far line. A flat best line means diminishing returns.
- `plot_param_importances(study)`: how much of the change in the score each parameter explains. Focus future tuning on the top few and fix the rest.
- `plot_slice(study)`: objective against each parameter. If good trials bunch up at the edge of a range, widen the range.
- `plot_contour(study, params=["lr", "depth"])`: interaction between two parameters.
- `plot_parallel_coordinate(study)`: all parameters at once.
- `plot_intermediate_values(study)`: learning curves of reported values, useful for checking pruning.
- `plot_pareto_front(study)`: for multi-objective studies.
- `plot_timeline(study)`: when each trial ran, showing which trials overlapped and which were slow.

The numbers behind the importance plot come from `optuna.importance.get_param_importances(study)`, which by default uses fANOVA, a statistical method that splits the score's variation between the settings; `PedAnovaImportanceEvaluator` is a fast alternative focusing on what distinguishes top trials.

Importance is relative to the ranges you searched: a parameter can look unimportant because its range was too narrow to matter.
concepts.code:
import optuna

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)

def objective(trial):
    lr = trial.suggest_float("lr", 1e-4, 1e-1, log=True)
    depth = trial.suggest_int("depth", 1, 10)
    noise = trial.suggest_float("unused_noise", 0, 1)   # barely matters
    return (lr * 100 - 1) ** 2 + (depth - 6) ** 2 * 0.5 + noise * 0.01

study = optuna.create_study(sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=0))
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=80)

imp = optuna.importance.get_param_importances(study)
print(list(imp)[-1])            # unused_noise  (least important)

fig = optuna.visualization.plot_optimization_history(study)
fig.write_html("history.html")  # or fig.show() in a notebook
optuna.visualization.plot_param_importances(study).write_html("importance.html")
optuna.visualization.plot_slice(study, params=["lr", "depth"]).write_html("slice.html")
takeaways: History, importance, slice and contour plots answer different questions
Use importances to decide which parameters to keep tuning
Good trials at a range edge mean the range should be widened
pitfalls: Concluding a parameter does not matter when its searched range was simply too narrow.

quiz.q: The slice plot shows all good trials at max_depth = 32, the top of the range. What should you do?
options: Widen the max_depth range and continue searching
quiz.explain: Optima at a boundary suggest the true optimum may lie outside the range.

concepts.name: Budgets, callbacks and enqueued trials
concepts.summary: Control how long a study runs, react to finished trials with callbacks, and seed the search with known-good parameters.
concepts.why: Real tuning runs need time budgets, early stopping of the whole study, and a head start from prior knowledge.
concepts.body:
`study.optimize` stops when either limit is reached:

- `n_trials=100`: number of trials in this call (not counting earlier ones in a resumed study).
- `timeout=3600`: seconds; the running trial finishes, no new one starts.

With neither, it runs until interrupted or `study.stop()` is called.

**Callbacks** are functions `callback(study, frozen_trial)` called after each trial, passed via `optimize(..., callbacks=[...])`. Uses include sending results to an experiment tracker such as MLflow, saving the best model, or stopping when no improvement happened for N trials by calling `study.stop()`. `optuna.study.MaxTrialsCallback(n, states=...)` caps the total number of trials across all **workers** (running copies of your script) that share one storage.

**Enqueue known configurations** with `study.enqueue_trial({"lr": 1e-3, "depth": 6})` before optimizing. The next trial uses those values instead of sampling (missing parameters are sampled), so defaults or previous best results are evaluated first and give the sampler a strong starting point.

Other useful options:

- `show_progress_bar=True` for a progress bar.
- `gc_after_trial=True` to run Python's **garbage collector** (which frees memory no longer in use) after each trial, for trials that use a lot of memory.
- `study.add_trial(optuna.trial.create_trial(params=..., distributions=..., value=...))` to import results computed outside Optuna.
takeaways: `n_trials` and `timeout` bound a run; `study.stop()` ends it from a callback
Callbacks receive (study, frozen_trial) after every trial
`enqueue_trial` evaluates chosen parameters before sampling starts
pitfalls: Expecting `timeout` to interrupt a running trial; it only prevents new trials from starting.

options: Fixes lr to 0.001 for all trials
Makes the next trial use lr=0.001 instead of sampling it
Adds a completed trial with lr=0.001
Removes lr from the search space
quiz.explain: Enqueued parameters are used by the next trial; afterwards normal sampling resumes.

concepts.name: Multi-objective optimization
concepts.summary: Optimize several objectives at once, such as accuracy and speed, and pick from the Pareto front.
concepts.why: Real models trade quality against cost, size or fairness; a single score hides those trade-offs.
concepts.body:
Pass `directions` instead of `direction` and return a tuple:

```python
study = optuna.create_study(directions=["maximize", "minimize"])
def objective(trial):
    ...
    return accuracy, latency_ms   # quality, and time per prediction
```

This is **multi-objective optimization**, and there is no single best trial anymore. `study.best_trials` returns the **Pareto front**: trials for which no other trial is at least as good on every objective and strictly better on one. Choosing among them is a business decision (e.g. the most accurate model that answers in under 20 ms).

Samplers: in Optuna 5 the default is TPE, which supports multiple objectives; `NSGAIISampler` (genetic) is a classic choice for larger budgets, `NSGAIIISampler` for many objectives, and `GPSampler` for small budgets.

Things that change:

- `trial.values` (plural) holds the objective tuple; `study.best_value` and `best_params` raise errors.
- Pruning is not supported for multi-objective studies.
- `optuna.visualization.plot_pareto_front(study, target_names=[...])` shows the trade-off curve.
- `study.set_metric_names(["accuracy", "latency_ms"])` labels objectives in plots and dataframes.

If one objective is really a hard limit (e.g. the model file must be under 50 MB), consider **constraints** instead: a `constraints_func` passed to the sampler marks trials as infeasible, which is simpler than exploring a full front.
concepts.code:
import optuna

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)

def objective(trial):
    n_layers = trial.suggest_int("n_layers", 1, 8)
    width = trial.suggest_int("width", 16, 512, log=True)
    accuracy = 1 - 1 / (1 + n_layers * width / 200)    # bigger is better...
    latency_ms = 0.5 + n_layers * width / 100           # ...but slower
    return accuracy, latency_ms

study = optuna.create_study(directions=["maximize", "minimize"],
                            sampler=optuna.samplers.NSGAIISampler(seed=0))
study.set_metric_names(["accuracy", "latency_ms"])
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=100)

front = sorted(study.best_trials, key=lambda t: t.values[1])
print(len(front) > 1)                       # True: several trade-offs
fast_enough = [t for t in front if t.values[1] <= 10]
best = max(fast_enough, key=lambda t: t.values[0])
print(best.params, [round(v, 3) for v in best.values])
takeaways: Use `directions=[...]` and return a tuple of values
`study.best_trials` is the Pareto front; pick from it with your own rule
No pruning in multi-objective studies; consider constraints for hard limits
pitfalls: Calling study.best_params on a multi-objective study, which raises an error.

quiz.q: What does study.best_trials contain in a two-objective study?
options: The single trial with the best first objective
The Pareto-optimal trials, none dominated by another
The top 10 trials by the sum of objectives
quiz.explain: best_trials returns the non-dominated set, representing the available trade-offs.

concepts.name: Parallel and distributed optimization
concepts.summary: Run trials at the same time with threads, several processes, or many machines sharing one storage.
concepts.why: Expensive trials only finish in reasonable time when many run at once.
concepts.body:
Optuna runs trials at the same time (in **parallel**) by having several workers share one study through storage. Each worker asks the storage for a new trial, the sampler reads the completed trials, and results are written back.

Three levels:

- **Threads** (parts of one program running side by side): `study.optimize(objective, n_trials=100, n_jobs=4)`. Easy, but Python's **GIL**, a lock that lets only one thread run Python code at a time, limits it.

Threads only help when the objective spends its time outside Python code: in NumPy or scikit-learn's compiled internals, training on a **GPU** (a graphics card used for fast maths), or waiting for files and the network.

- **Processes on one machine**: start the same script several times; each running copy is a separate **process**. Each calls `create_study(..., storage=..., load_if_exists=True)` and `optimize`. Use JournalStorage with a file, or a database.
- **Many machines**: point all workers at PostgreSQL or MySQL. For very many workers, put a gRPC **proxy** server (a go-between that passes requests on to the database) in front of it, via `run_grpc_proxy_server` and `GrpcStorageProxy`.

Kubernetes jobs or a **cluster** scheduler (software that runs work on a group of machines) simply launch N copies.

Caveats:

- Model-based samplers lose some efficiency when many trials run at once, since they can't learn from unfinished ones. TPE's `constant_liar` option (on by default in Optuna 5) treats running trials as if they had a poor result, so workers don't all sample the same region.
- Use `MaxTrialsCallback` to cap the total number of trials, because each worker's `n_trials` counts only its own.
- Don't rely on seeds to repeat parallel runs exactly.
- Turn on heartbeats so trials from crashed workers don't stay RUNNING forever.
concepts.code:
import optuna
from optuna.storages import JournalStorage
from optuna.storages.journal import JournalFileBackend
from optuna.study import MaxTrialsCallback
from optuna.trial import TrialState

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)

def objective(trial):
    x = trial.suggest_float("x", -10, 10)
    return (x - 1) ** 2

# Each worker process runs this same code (e.g. `python tune.py` started 4 times).
storage = JournalStorage(JournalFileBackend("parallel_journal.log"))
study = optuna.create_study(study_name="shared", storage=storage, load_if_exists=True)
study.optimize(
    objective,
    n_jobs=2,                                 # threads inside this worker
    callbacks=[MaxTrialsCallback(40, states=(TrialState.COMPLETE,))],
)
print(len(study.get_trials(states=(TrialState.COMPLETE,))) >= 40)   # True
takeaways: Workers coordinate only through shared storage
`n_jobs` uses threads (GIL-bound); separate processes or machines scale further
Cap total trials with MaxTrialsCallback; constant_liar reduces duplicate sampling
pitfalls: Expecting n_jobs=8 to speed up a pure-Python objective; threads share the GIL, so use processes.

quiz.q: Four worker processes each call optimize(n_trials=50) on the same shared study. How many trials run in total?
quiz.explain: n_trials counts per optimize call, so each of the four workers runs 50; use MaxTrialsCallback for a global cap.

concepts.name: Ask-and-tell and integrations
concepts.summary: Drive Optuna from your own loop with ask and tell, and use integrations for LightGBM, PyTorch Lightning and trackers.
concepts.why: When another tool or system runs the training, you need Optuna without writing an objective function.
concepts.body:
`study.optimize` assumes Optuna calls your objective. The **ask-and-tell** interface inverts control:

```python
trial = study.ask()                 # new trial
lr = trial.suggest_float("lr", 1e-5, 1e-1, log=True)
score = run_somewhere(lr)           # your loop, job queue, external system
study.tell(trial, score)            # or state=TrialState.PRUNED / FAIL
```

This fits training scripts that cannot be wrapped in a function, scoring several trials together as one **batch**, or setups where results come back at unpredictable times. You can also pass a **fixed distribution dict** to `study.ask({"lr": FloatDistribution(1e-5, 1e-1, log=True)})` to define the space up front.

**Integrations** live in the separate `optuna-integration` package (`pip install optuna-integration[...]`):

- `LightGBMTunerCV` tunes LightGBM's key parameters stepwise.
- Pruning callbacks for XGBoost, LightGBM, PyTorch Lightning, Keras and others call `trial.report`/`should_prune` for you from inside the framework's training loop.
- `MLflowCallback` and `WeightsAndBiasesCallback` log every trial to your tracker.

Other frameworks integrate the other way around: Hugging Face `Trainer.hyperparameter_search(backend="optuna")` and Ray Tune's `OptunaSearch` use Optuna as their search engine.

Whatever the interface, the study, samplers, pruners and storage behave identically.
concepts.code:
import optuna
from optuna.distributions import FloatDistribution, IntDistribution

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)
study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize",
                            sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=0))
space = {"lr": FloatDistribution(1e-4, 1e-1, log=True),
         "batch": IntDistribution(16, 128, log=True)}

def external_training(lr, batch):          # stand-in for any training system
    return 0.9 - abs(lr - 0.01) * 5 - abs(batch - 64) / 1000

for round_ in range(5):                      # e.g. launch 4 jobs at a time
    trials = [study.ask(space) for _ in range(4)]
    for t in trials:
        score = external_training(t.params["lr"], t.params["batch"])
        study.tell(t, score)

print(len(study.trials), round(study.best_value, 3))   # 20 and a value near 0.9
takeaways: `ask()` creates a trial, `tell(trial, value)` finishes it
Pass a distribution dict to `ask` to define the space without suggest calls
optuna-integration provides pruning callbacks and tracker callbacks
pitfalls: Forgetting to call tell for an asked trial, leaving it RUNNING and confusing samplers and counts.

quiz.q: When is ask-and-tell preferable to study.optimize?
options: Never; it is a deprecated API
When an external loop or system controls training and you cannot wrap it in an objective
quiz.explain: Ask-and-tell lets your own code or infrastructure decide when and how trials run.

concepts.name: How TPE works
concepts.summary: Understand the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator: good/bad splits, density ratios, multivariate modelling and constant liar.
concepts.why: Knowing TPE's mechanics explains its behaviour on small budgets, conditional spaces and parallel runs, and which options to tune.
concepts.body:
Most Bayesian optimization models `p(score | params)`: how likely each score is for given values. TPE turns this around and models the values given the score:

1. After `n_startup_trials` random trials, sort completed trials by objective value and split them into a **good** group (the top fraction, controlled by `gamma`) and a **bad** group.
2. Fit two **probability densities** (curves of where values are common) over the parameter values: `l(x)` from good trials and `g(x)` from bad trials. Each is a Parzen estimator: a sum of **kernels**, small bumps centred on the observed values, plus one broad bump covering the whole range.
3. Draw `n_ei_candidates` samples from `l(x)` and choose the one maximizing `l(x) / g(x)`, which is proportional to the **expected improvement**: how much a candidate is expected to beat the best score so far.

Consequences:

- **Independent vs multivariate**: classic TPE models each parameter separately and misses interactions. Optuna 5 enables multivariate TPE by default for single-objective studies, modelling parameters jointly. `group=True` additionally decomposes conditional spaces into subspaces that are modelled jointly.
- **Conditional spaces** are natural because each parameter's density only uses trials where it was sampled.
- **Startup**: the first trials are random, so very small budgets gain little from TPE.
- **Parallelism**: with `constant_liar=True` running trials are treated as bad results, discouraging other workers from sampling the same spot.
- **Categoricals** use weighted category frequencies rather than kernels.

TPE's cost per trial grows with the number of completed trials but stays small, which is why it scales to thousands of trials where Gaussian-process samplers become slow.
concepts.code:
import optuna

optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)

def objective(trial):                       # strong interaction between x and y
    x = trial.suggest_float("x", -5, 5)
    y = trial.suggest_float("y", -5, 5)
    return (x - y) ** 2 + 0.1 * (x + y - 4) ** 2

def run(**kw):
    vals = []
    for seed in range(5):
        s = optuna.create_study(sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=seed, **kw))
        s.optimize(objective, n_trials=60)
        vals.append(s.best_value)
    return sum(vals) / len(vals)

print(f"independent : {run(multivariate=False):.3f}")
print(f"multivariate: {run(multivariate=True):.3f}")   # usually lower (better)
print(f"short warmup: {run(multivariate=True, n_startup_trials=5):.3f}")
takeaways: TPE splits trials into good and bad and maximizes the density ratio l(x)/g(x)
Multivariate TPE (default for single objective in Optuna 5) captures parameter interactions
constant_liar improves parallel runs; the first n_startup_trials are random
pitfalls: Expecting TPE to beat random search with only 10 to 15 trials, when most of them are random startup trials.

quiz.q: In TPE, which candidate parameter values are preferred?
options: Those farthest from all previous trials
Those with the highest density under bad trials
Those maximizing l(x)/g(x): likely under good trials, unlikely under bad ones
quiz.explain: The ratio of good-trial to bad-trial densities is proportional to expected improvement.

concepts.name: Custom samplers, pruners and constraints
concepts.summary: Extend Optuna with your own sampler or pruner classes and handle constrained optimization.
concepts.why: Research ideas, domain-specific search strategies and hard constraints all require going beyond built-ins.
concepts.body:
**Custom samplers** subclass `optuna.samplers.BaseSampler` and implement three methods:

- `infer_relative_search_space(study, trial)`: which parameters to sample jointly (return `{}` to sample everything independently),
- `sample_relative(study, trial, search_space)`: joint sampling for that space, returning a dict,
- `sample_independent(study, trial, param_name, param_distribution)`: one parameter at a time, for parameters outside the relative space (for example ones discovered during define-by-run).

Read history with `study.get_trials(deepcopy=False, states=...)`. Many custom samplers delegate `sample_independent` to a `RandomSampler`.

**Custom pruners** subclass `BasePruner` and implement `prune(study, trial) -> bool`, using `trial.intermediate_values` and other trials' values. They plug into `should_prune` unchanged.

**Constraints**: TPE, NSGA-II/III and GP samplers accept `constraints_func(frozen_trial) -> sequence of floats`, where a value of 0 or less means satisfied. Store the constraint quantities as user attributes inside the objective and read them back in the function. Infeasible trials still complete but are deprioritized, and `best_trials` (multi-objective) or your own filtering returns feasible ones.

**Ablation and reuse**: `optuna.samplers.PartialFixedSampler` fixes some parameters while another sampler handles the rest, and `optuna.copy_study` or `add_trials` move history between studies, for example to warm-start a related problem.
takeaways: BaseSampler: infer_relative_search_space, sample_relative, sample_independent
BasePruner: implement prune(study, trial) using intermediate values
constraints_func returns values <= 0 for satisfied constraints
pitfalls: Returning values outside the distribution's bounds from a custom sampler, which Optuna rejects.

quiz.q: In a constraints_func, what does returning [0.3] for a trial mean?
quiz.explain: Values greater than zero indicate violation; zero or negative means feasible.

concepts.name: Fault tolerance: heartbeats and retries
concepts.summary: Keep long studies spread over many machines healthy when workers crash or are stopped, using heartbeats, stale-trial checks and retries.
concepts.why: On cheap interruptible cloud machines and shared clusters, workers die mid-trial; without heartbeats those trials hang as RUNNING forever.
concepts.body:
When a worker process is killed (it ran out of memory, the cloud provider took the machine back, or the hardware failed), its trial never reports back. Without extra setup it stays `RUNNING` forever: it spoils counts, `MaxTrialsCallback` miscounts, and the sampler may treat it as still in progress.

Heartbeats solve this for RDB storage:

```python
storage = optuna.storages.RDBStorage(
    url, heartbeat_interval=60, grace_period=120,
    heartbeat_stale_trial_callback=RetryHeartbeatStaleTrialCallback(max_retry=3))
```

- Each running trial records a heartbeat every `heartbeat_interval` seconds from a background thread.
- A trial whose last heartbeat is older than `grace_period` is a **stale trial**. Other workers check for stale trials when they start a new trial (or you call `optuna.storages.fail_stale_trials(study)`), and mark them `FAIL`.
- `RetryHeartbeatStaleTrialCallback(max_retry=3)` then queues the same parameters again as a `WAITING` trial, so the configuration is **retried**. `RetryHeartbeatStaleTrialCallback.retried_trial_number(trial)` and `retry_history(trial)` link retries to the original. It replaces the older `RetryFailedTrialCallback`, **deprecated** (kept but being phased out) since 4.9.

Other robustness practices:

- Make objectives **idempotent**, so running one twice does no more harm than running it once, and save **checkpoints** (copies of the model partway through training) named by trial number, so a retry can resume. Store their paths in user attributes.
- Treat expected failures inside the objective (`catch=`, returning NaN) separately from machine failures (heartbeats).

- Keep the database healthy: reuse its connections with a **connection pool** (set through `engine_kwargs`), put a gRPC proxy in front for hundreds of workers, and take regular backups.
- Clean up abandoned studies with `optuna.delete_study`.
concepts.code:
import multiprocessing as mp
import time
import optuna
from optuna.storages import RDBStorage, RetryHeartbeatStaleTrialCallback

def make_storage():
    return RDBStorage("sqlite:///ft_demo.db", heartbeat_interval=1, grace_period=3,
        heartbeat_stale_trial_callback=RetryHeartbeatStaleTrialCallback(max_retry=2))

def worker():                                 # a trial that never finishes
    study = optuna.load_study(study_name="ft", storage=make_storage())
    study.optimize(lambda t: time.sleep(t.suggest_float("x", 0, 1) + 60), n_trials=1)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    optuna.logging.set_verbosity(optuna.logging.WARNING)
    study = optuna.create_study(study_name="ft", storage=make_storage())
    p = mp.Process(target=worker); p.start(); time.sleep(4)
    p.kill()                                  # simulate preemption mid-trial
    time.sleep(4)                             # heartbeat goes stale
    optuna.storages.fail_stale_trials(study)  # other workers do this automatically
    print([t.state.name for t in study.get_trials()])   # ['FAIL', 'WAITING']
    retry = study.get_trials()[-1]
    print(RetryHeartbeatStaleTrialCallback.retried_trial_number(retry))   # 0
    optuna.delete_study(study_name="ft", storage=make_storage())
takeaways: Without heartbeats, crashed trials stay RUNNING forever
Stale trials (no heartbeat within grace_period) are marked FAIL by other workers
RetryHeartbeatStaleTrialCallback re-queues their parameters as WAITING trials
pitfalls: Setting grace_period shorter than the heartbeat interval plus normal delays, so healthy trials get marked stale.

quiz.q: A preempted worker leaves a trial RUNNING. With heartbeats and RetryHeartbeatStaleTrialCallback configured, what eventually happens?
options: Nothing until the study is deleted
Another worker marks it FAIL and enqueues a WAITING retry with the same parameters
It is marked COMPLETE with value 0
quiz.explain: Stale detection fails the trial and the callback re-enqueues its parameters for another attempt.
